drapeaux.note: Le Chapelier's speech of June 14, 1791 is in French; no published English translation was found, so the passage is translated from the French.

titre: A 1791 Law Founds Freedom of Labor by Forbidding Workers to Unite
accroche: France, June 14, 1791: the Le Chapelier law proclaims freedom of labor and, in the same text, forbids workers to associate to discuss their wages.
contenu_vulgarise:
Paris, June 14, 1791. The National Constituent Assembly votes a decree introduced by the Breton deputy Isaac Le Chapelier, a lawyer by trade. The text bears a plain title: law on assemblies of workers and artisans of the same trade and profession. It completes the Allarde decree, passed three months earlier, which abolishes the guilds and proclaims freedom of enterprise. In a single spring, the two texts close a century of regulation of the trades.

## A Freedom That Does Not Allow Union

From the rostrum, Le Chapelier presents his law as the logical sequel to this regained freedom. Since guilds no longer exist, he explains, there must no longer be any collective interest among citizens of the same profession, only the private interest of each person and the general interest: “there is no longer any guild in the State, there is only the private interest of each individual, and the general interest.” He adds that one must “go back to the principle that it is for free agreements between individuals to set the day's wage for each worker.”

The text as voted forbids any assembly of citizens of the same status or profession, whether it comes from masters or from workers. Article IV punishes anyone who takes part in a collective deliberation on wages with a fine of five hundred livres and a one-year suspension of the rights of an active citizen; Article VI raises the penalty to a fine of one thousand livres and three months in prison if the deliberation contains threats against workers who would agree to work for a lower wage. Article VIII goes further: a gathering of workers seeking to bear on “the freedom that the constitution grants to labor and industry” is classed as a seditious gathering, the same criminal category as riots.

## What the Word Freedom Covers

The same word thus designates two opposite measures depending on who exercises it. The master gains the freedom to open a workshop without a master's letter; the worker loses the right to discuss his wages collectively, something he could do, unequally, inside the guild that has just been dissolved. What closes is not only the hierarchy of trades of the Ancien Régime. It is all collective bargaining, including whatever a balance of power more favorable to workers might one day have produced.

The law does not disappear quickly. On April 12, 1803, a new text, the one that establishes the workers' booklet (livret ouvrier), renews the ban on coalitions. The 1810 penal code takes it up in turn in its Articles 414 and 415. It takes until May 25, 1864 for a first law, known as the Ollivier law, to end the offense of coalition without yet authorizing unions, and then March 21, 1884 for the Waldeck-Rousseau law to legalize them. Ninety-three years separate the original vote from this second date. In Belgium, which remained under its sway after independence, the text stays in force until 1867.

A question remains that goes beyond French labor law: a freedom proclaimed for everyone does not necessarily benefit equally all those who might exercise it. Whenever it is invoked, it is worth asking whose freedom it extends, and whose it closes.

carte.punch: The same word, freedom, lets the master open a shop and forbids the worker to unite.
carte.idee: In 1791, the Le Chapelier law proclaims freedom of labor by abolishing the guilds, but in the same text forbids anyone in the same trade to assemble to bargain collectively over working conditions, on pain of a fine and suspension of the rights of an active citizen.

quiz.question: What does a French worker or artisan lose in June 1791, the same year the Le Chapelier law proclaims freedom of labor?
choix: The right to choose an employer freely, now subject to the approval of municipal authorities
The right to assemble with other workers of the same trade to discuss wages collectively
The right to practice a trade without a master's letter from a guild
The right to bring an employer to court for non-payment of wages
quiz.explication: The law forbids any collective assembly of citizens of the same trade, on pain of a fine and suspension of the rights of an active citizen. The right to practice a trade without a master's letter is not taken away but granted, the same year, by the Allarde decree.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Isaac Le Chapelier's profession before he introduced the decree of June 14, 1791?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Isaac Le Chapelier, the Breton deputy who introduced this decree in the National Constituent Assembly, was a lawyer.

quiz_supplementaire.question: The decree of June 14, 1791 completes another text, passed three months earlier. Which one?
choix: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
The decree establishing the income tax
The Allarde decree, on freedom of enterprise
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry notes that this decree completes the Allarde decree, passed three months earlier, which abolishes the guilds and proclaims freedom of enterprise.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the text cited in the entry, what penalty does Article IV set for an ordinary collective deliberation on wages?
choix: A 500-livre fine and a one-year suspension of the rights of an active citizen
A 1,000-livre fine and three months of actual imprisonment
Total confiscation of property and permanent banishment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that Article IV punishes ordinary collective deliberation with a 500-livre fine and a one-year suspension of the rights of an active citizen; the 1,000 livres and three months in prison apply only to the aggravated case of threats against replacement workers, covered by Article VI.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Until what year does the 1791 text remain in force in Belgium, which stayed under its sway after independence?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that in Belgium the law stays in force until 1867, whereas in France the offense of coalition ends as early as 1864 with the Ollivier law.
